summary: Adds two response codes, SYS and AUTH, to POP3, plus a capability named AUTH-RESP-CODE. They let a mail client tell whether a login failure is a temporary system problem or an authentication problem, so it can react sensibly. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When a mailbox refuses you, you want to know if the lock is broken or if you have the wrong key. These new messages tell the mail program which one it is.

subtitle: Two POP3 error codes and a capability that tell a mail client whether a failed login is the user's fault or the server's.

tldr.problem: When a POP3 login fails, the client often cannot tell whether the user's credentials are wrong or the server has some other trouble, so it may nag the user for a password it should not ask for.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the SYS response code (with TEMP and PERM sub-codes) for system errors and the AUTH response code for credential problems, plus an AUTH-RESP-CODE capability that promises the server uses AUTH for every credential error.
tldr.outcome: A client can unambiguously pick the right reaction: ask for new credentials, retry later, or tell the user to contact support. It is a Proposed Standard and nothing in the metadata says it was replaced.

facts.label: New response codes
facts.value: SYS (with TEMP and PERM) and AUTH

today: RFC 3206 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the extension mechanism of RFC 2449.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2449 gave POP3 a mechanism for extended response codes, so a server can say more about an error than a bare -ERR. It defined two initial codes, IN-USE and LOGIN-DELAY, to separate credential failures from other errors.

RFC 3206 says these two codes, while helpful, do not go far enough. It adds two more response codes, SYS and AUTH, and one new capability, AUTH-RESP-CODE. Together they let a client work out the best response to an authentication failure without guessing.
sections.eli5: Mail servers could already say a little about why they said no. This memo adds two clearer reasons: the server is having a problem, or your login is the problem.

sections.title: Why IN-USE and LOGIN-DELAY Were Not Enough
sections.content:
The point of response codes is to let a client see the real cause of a failure. For example, a client needs to know whether to ask the user for new credentials or simply to try the POP3 session again later. Some deployed POP3 clients had been parsing the text of failure messages, looking for strings that various servers use to say a mailbox is locked.

IN-USE means an exclusive lock on the user's mailbox could not be obtained, probably because another POP3 session is in progress. LOGIN-DELAY means the user has not waited long enough before authenticating again.

Other error conditions do not need new credentials, and some of them should be brought to the user's attention. Even with the two older codes, a client could not be sure whether any other error required new credentials.
sections.eli5: Before, mail programs had to read the words of an error message and guess. That is like guessing why a door is locked by squinting at the sign on it.

sections.title: The SYS Response Code
sections.content:
SYS announces that a failure is due to a system error, as opposed to the user's credentials or an external condition. It is hierarchical, with two second-level codes, TEMP and PERM. Case does not matter at any level.

  • SYS/TEMP signals a problem likely to be temporary, so there is no need to alarm the user unless it persists. Examples are a central resource that is locked or unavailable, or insufficient free disk or memory.
  • SYS/PERM signals a problem unlikely to be resolved without intervention. It is appropriate to alert the user and suggest contacting the organization's support personnel. Examples are corrupted mailboxes and system configuration errors.

The SYS code is valid with an -ERR response to any command.
sections.eli5: SYS means the problem is on the server's side. TEMP says wait a bit and it will probably fix itself, and PERM says someone needs to fix it, so call for help.

sections.title: The AUTH Response Code
sections.content:
AUTH tells the client that there is a problem with the user's credentials. That might be an incorrect password, an unknown user name, an expired account, an attempt to authenticate against policy (such as from an invalid location or at an unauthorized time), or some other problem.

It is valid with an -ERR response to any authentication command, including AUTH, USER, PASS or APOP.

Returning AUTH in reply to the USER command reveals to the client that the specified user exists. The RFC strongly RECOMMENDS that the server not issue this response code to USER.
sections.eli5: AUTH means the problem is with you: the wrong password, an unknown name, or a login that is not allowed right now. The server is careful not to say it too early, because that could tell a stranger which names are real.

sections.title: The AUTH-RESP-CODE Capability
sections.content:
Servers that include the AUTH response code with any authentication failure SHOULD support the CAPA command and SHOULD include the AUTH-RESP-CODE capability in the CAPA response. The capability assures the client that only errors carrying the AUTH code are caused by credential problems.

The capability definition follows the template from RFC 2449. It takes no arguments, adds no commands and affects no standard commands. It is announced in both states, with no difference between them. In short, it indicates that the server includes AUTH with any authentication error caused by a problem with the user's credentials.
sections.eli5: AUTH-RESP-CODE is a promise on the server's door. It says: if I say AUTH, it is really your login, and if I do not say AUTH, it is not.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has added the AUTH-RESP-CODE capability to the list of POP3 capabilities, and the SYS and AUTH response codes to the list of POP3 response codes. Both lists were established by RFC 2449.

The Security Considerations section is a single pointer: the security issue is the one in the section on the AUTH response code, namely that issuing it for the USER command reveals that a user exists.
sections.eli5: The only safety worry is that a helpful error could tell a stranger which user names are real, so servers should not say AUTH at that step.

viz.caption: POP3 RESPONSE CODES ADDED BY RFC 3206

items.label: Temporary system problem
items.desc: Likely temporary; do not alarm the user unless it persists.

items.label: Permanent system problem
items.desc: Unlikely to be resolved without intervention; suggest contacting support.

items.label: Credential problem
items.desc: Wrong password, unknown user, expired account or policy violation.
